# Affine cone profiles: the full two-mixture inequality

This is a proved special case of the orientation-separated profile criterion. It covers arbitrary centered probability laws of slopes, not only the layer marginals supplied by a convex base. It is an exact functional consequence of the even-unimodal truncation inequality proved in `candidate 2be89ee8039bb5fd`. No reduction of general profiles to cones is claimed.

Let d=m+1>=2, H>0, B=H+1, and

    r(z)=(H-z)/B,     -1<=z<=H.

Use the planar measure f(x,z)=r(z)^(m-1)/2 on |x|<=r(z). Its mass and its horizontal raw coarea are

    V=B/d,       C0=(H/B)^m.

Let P(s),C(s),M(s) be the physical cap, raw coarea, and vertical section moment for z+s x>=0. For any probability law mu on finite nonnegative slopes, write bars for its averages, and suppose Mbar=0. Then the SAME number

    c=(V/C0)[(H/B)^d-4/9]                         (1)

works for every such mu:

    (4/9)V <= Pbar-c Cbar <= (5/9)V.              (2)

Consequently any two separately centered slope laws mu,nu satisfy

    [Cbar_nu Pbar_mu+Cbar_mu(V-Pbar_nu)]
       /[V(Cbar_mu+Cbar_nu)] >=4/9,              (3)

whenever the denominator is positive. In particular the desired Gamma_d comparison holds for this profile, since Gamma_d<=4/9 for d>=2.

## 1. A common even base law

A slope s is equivalent to a base variable b uniform on [-s,s]; at s=0 use the point mass at zero. Indeed substituting x=r(z)u, -1<=u<=1, changes f dx dz into r(z)^m du dz/2, and the cap becomes

    z+r(z)b>=0,       b=s u.

Mixing in s gives one even unimodal probability law phi in b, a mixture of those uniform laws and a possible atom at zero. No relation between different mu laws is imposed.

Put

    v=phi{b<=1},
    e(a)=int_(b<=1) (1-a b)^(-d)dphi(b),  0<a<1,
    a0=1/B,      p0=(H/B)^d.

Here 1/2<v<=1. Every finite uniform layer has strictly more than half its mass below 1; averaging retains strictness. Along a fixed base ray, use t=r(z), so z=H-Bt and 0<=t<=1. If b>=1, the whole ray is captured. If b<1, its captured part is 0<=t<=H/(B-b). Direct integration yields

    Pbar/V=p0 e(a0)+1-v,
    Cbar/C0=e(a0),
    Mbar/C0=-(H/B)int_(b<=1)b(1-b/B)^(-d-1)dphi(b).   (4)

The coarea formula follows by dividing the ray density r(z)^m by the derivative 1-b/B of the margin along z. At b=1 the root is at the base endpoint; phi has no atom there, so its convention does not change these integrals.

The function e is convex on (0,1). Its derivatives on a compact subinterval are justified by bounded domination: b is bounded above by 1, and its negative tail is damped by the positive denominator. The third formula in (4) and Mbar=0 give e'(a0)=0. Hence e(a0)<=e(a) for every 0<a<1. If v=1, the captured support is symmetric and bounded by 1, so a=0 is also an admissible comparison.

## 2. The exact energy interval, including an atom and unbounded layers

The even-unimodal layer proof applies directly to the present mixture law:

    2v-1 <= e(a0) <= (2v-1)/v.                   (5)

For the lower bound, restrict to the symmetric interval [-1,1], whose phi mass is 2v-1. Pairing b and -b, or Jensen, shows that every positive affine denominator has inverse-power average at least one on this symmetric part.

For completeness, the upper-bound proof needs neither a bounded density nor compact support. If v<1, put k=1-v and compare e(a0) with e(2k/d). For a uniform layer [-s,s], let x=min(1/s,1), with x=1 for s=0. Its captured fraction is (1+x)/2, so E x=2v-1. At exponent 2, its integral with denominator 1-kb is bounded above by

    I_k(x)=x(1+x)/[2(1-k)(x+k)].

For s>=1 this is exact integration. For 0<s<1 the full-layer integral is 1/[1-k^2 s^2]<=I_k(1); the atom s=0 gives 1<=I_k(1) as well. Since I_k''(x)=-k/(x+k)^3<0, Jensen gives the bound I_k(2v-1)=(2v-1)/v. The elementary exponent comparison

    (1-(2k/d)b)^(-d) <= (1-kb)^(-2),  b<=1,

holds for d>=2 and was proved by differentiating p -> -p log(1+a/p). All denominators are uniformly positive on b<=1, including its unbounded negative part. Thus integration over any mixture of finite layers is justified directly and proves the upper bound. If v=1, use e(a0)<=e(0)=1. This proves (5) in the full stated scope.

## 3. Common correction and the two-law payment

Equations (1) and (4) give

    (Pbar-c Cbar)/V=1-v+(4/9)e(a0).

Its lower bound from (5) is (5-v)/9>=4/9. Its upper bound is at most 5/9, because

    5/9-[1-v+(4/9)(2v-1)/v]=(3v-2)^2/(9v)>=0.

This proves (2). Multiply its lower inequality for mu by Cbar_nu and its upper inequality for nu by Cbar_mu; the two c terms cancel, giving (3).

If the slope line is compactified with an atom at infinity, that atom has the limiting records P=V/2,C=M=0. It already satisfies (2). Splitting it from the finite law therefore extends the result to such laws as well; it is not interpreted as a uniform probability measure on an infinite interval.

This proves the arbitrary-layer two-law comparison for an affine cone profile. A general truncated affine frustum or a profile with changing slope is not reduced to this case by the present argument.

# Affine cone profiles: the full two-mixture inequality

**Affine cone two-mixture inequality for arbitrary centered slope laws**

Let d>=2 and H>0. On -1<=z<=H, |x|<=r(z), r(z)=(H-z)/(H+1), use density r(z)^(d-2)/2 and the physical cap/coarea/moment records P(s),C(s),M(s) for z+s x>=0, with 0<=s<infinity. Put V=(H+1)/d, C0=(H/(H+1))^(d-1), and c=(V/C0)[(H/(H+1))^d-4/9]. Every probability law on these nonnegative slopes with mean record Mbar=0 satisfies 4V/9<=Pbar-c Cbar<=5V/9. The limiting infinity record (P,C,M)=(V/2,0,0) is also allowed. Two separately centered laws mu,nu therefore satisfy [Cbar_nu Pbar_mu+Cbar_mu(V-Pbar_nu)]/[V(Cbar_mu+Cbar_nu)]>=4/9 whenever Cbar_mu+Cbar_nu>0; when both are the infinity record the corresponding cap fraction is 1/2.

Scope limits: Covers arbitrary finite-layer mixtures, an atom at zero and the limiting infinity record (P,C,M)=(V/2,0,0). It does not reduce arbitrary profiles to cones.
